purpose: Atazanavir is used to treat HIV, the virus that causes AIDS. It is always used together with other HIV medicines as part of a combination treatment plan. It helps keep the HIV virus under control so your immune system can stay stronger and healthier.
how_it_works: HIV needs a special tool called a protease enzyme to make copies of itself inside your body. Atazanavir blocks that tool, so the virus cannot make new copies of itself. This lowers the amount of HIV in your blood and helps protect your immune system from further damage.
common_side_effects: Your skin or the whites of your eyes may turn slightly yellow — this is common and usually harmless. You might also notice nausea, stomach pain, headache, or diarrhea. Some people develop a rash in the first few weeks of treatment.
warnings: Tell your doctor about all medicines you take, because atazanavir can interact with many drugs including heartburn medicines, cholesterol medicines, and blood thinners. It can affect your heart rhythm, so tell your doctor if you have any heart problems. It may also raise blood sugar or affect kidney function, so regular checkups are important. Never stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.
typical_dosing: The usual adult dose is 300 mg once a day taken WITH a low-dose booster medicine called ritonavir (100 mg) or cobicistat. Always take it WITH food to help your body absorb it properly. Try to take it at the same time every day.
